name: Title 1
text: Understanding and Applying DevOps Principles

name: Subtitle 2
text:
COMP2013 - Lab 2
A practical transformation plan

Reference case-study presentation. The case organization is hypothetical. The proposed actions, timing, allocations and targets are design choices, not observed results. Sources: [1] Lab 2 brief; [2] Lecture 02. The supplied template provides the presentation structure.

name: Title 1
text: Team details

name: members-label
text: Team members

name: members
text:
Qixuan Yang (20719443)
Ronghao Hu (20719451)
Hanbo Zhao (20719456)

name: team-admin-label
text: Team name / number

name: team-admin
text: Not provided - complete before submission

Student names and IDs were provided by the user. No team name, number or contribution allocation was provided. Do not infer the three students are the organizational role owners in the transformation plan.

name: Title 1
text: Background of the organization

name: block-1-label
text: People and products

name: block-1-text
text: About 100 people at one site; three development teams of 10-15 people. Three web applications share a common database.

name: block-2-label
text: Current delivery process

name: block-2-text
text: Sales gathers requirements; teams use their own processes and tools. Development performs functional tests; Test performs manual integration and acceptance tests; Operations deploys to Google Cloud.

name: block-3-label
text: Communication

name: block-3-text
text: Informal email is the primary channel. The business domain and current delivery performance are not specified.

Source [1], pp. 1-2. These are case facts. The three applications share some data through a common database; the brief does not say every table or service is shared. The organization diagram has CEO, Staff, Development, Test, Operations, Sales and other departments.

name: Title 1
text: Task 1 - Challenge register

name: table-footnote
text: Consequences are reasoned possibilities. The assumptions behind them are stated next.

preview: ID / challenge | Case evidence | Potential consequence | Plan response

text: Source [1], pp. 1-2. This register separates given evidence from possible effects. C4 is a risk hypothesis: organizational separation does not by itself prove a blame culture. P1-P4 and L1-L3 are tracked through subsequent slides.

name: Title 1
text: Task 1 - Communication and trust

name: block-1-label
text: C1: assumptions

name: block-1-text
text: A1: there is no shared, authoritative backlog or decision log. A2: important release decisions are held in individual inboxes.

name: block-2-label
text: C1: implications

name: block-2-text
text: Teams may implement different priorities or lose context at handoffs. A shared backlog, named product owner and documented release decisions would reduce ambiguity.

name: block-3-label
text: C4: assumption and implication

name: block-3-text
text: A3: Dev is rewarded for features and Ops for uptime. If true, conflicting incentives discourage risk reporting and sharing. Validate through interviews; introduce shared outcomes and no-blame reviews.

Sources: [1], pp. 1-2; [2], lecture slides 24, 26, 42-44. A1-A3 are explicit assumptions, not stated case facts. Week 1 interviews include representatives from all departments and the CEO; inspect current tools and incentives. If an adequate shared backlog exists, improve it rather than replace it. If incentives are already aligned, retain them. Knowledge creation: record competing perspectives in a value-stream map and shared decisions.

name: Title 1
text: Task 1 - Tools and shared data

name: block-1-label
text: C2: assumptions

name: block-1-text
text: A4: teams have incompatible build or release conventions. A5: one application can introduce database changes that affect the other two.

name: block-2-label
text: Implications

name: block-2-text
text: Integration defects may appear late; a database change can block several releases. Tool differences may duplicate work and make troubleshooting harder.

name: block-3-label
text: Response and trade-off

name: block-3-text
text: Agree minimum build/test checks and versioned migration rules. Test all three applications against changed schemas. Keep useful team tools; defer a full database split because cost and feasibility are unknown.

Source [1], pp. 1-2; [2], lecture slides 28, 37-38. A4-A5 are assumptions. Shared storage is a stated fact, but incompatible release conventions and breaking schema changes are not confirmed. P2 and P3 address these risks. Compatibility policy: add compatible columns or tables first, migrate callers, then remove old schema only when all applications are verified. Backups, restore rehearsals and contract tests are necessary before production changes. A complete database separation is not assumed achievable within 12 weeks.

name: Title 1
text: Task 1 - Testing and release queues

name: block-1-label
text: C3: assumptions

name: block-1-text
text: A6: the Test team has limited capacity and repeated regression work. A7: deployment depends on manual steps and person-specific knowledge.

name: block-2-label
text: Implications

name: block-2-text
text: Work waits between teams; large release batches increase rework and recovery effort. Faster development alone can enlarge the test queue.

name: block-3-label
text: Response and trade-off

name: block-3-text
text: Measure queue time first. Automate critical regression checks, retain exploratory acceptance tests, and limit work in progress. Give the pilot squad joint responsibility for release readiness.

Source [1], p. 2; [2], lecture slides 28-36, 58-60. Manual integration/acceptance testing and the Test-to-Ops handoff are given. Capacity limitations and manual deployment are assumptions. If deployment is already automated, retain it and document missing checks. A CI/CD platform alone does not solve the queue. Test specialists help developers create repeatable tests, then focus manual work on exploratory and user acceptance testing. Value-stream analysis should distinguish touch time from waiting time.

name: Title 1
text: Task 2 - Objectives and approach

name: block-1-label
text: First Way: flow across the whole system

name: block-1-text
text: Make work visible, limit work in progress, reduce batch sizes and handoffs, then improve the measured constraint.

name: block-2-label
text: Proposed 12-week outcomes

name: block-2-text
text: Pilot: halve median commit-to-production time; deploy at least weekly; do not worsen the change failure rate; demonstrate rollback within 10 minutes. Baselines are unknown until weeks 1-2.

name: block-3-label
text: Pilot before scaling

name: block-3-text
text: Select one application and one critical user journey. Continue normal development; reserve pilot capacity rather than stop the whole company. Broader rollout depends on the pilot evidence.

Sources: [1], Task 2; [2], lecture slides 27-36 and 61. All numerical outcomes are proposed, not measured or promised. Compare representative changes, report sample counts and investigate small samples. The 12-week plan assumes CEO support, access to code/cloud systems and a suitable pilot; confirm in week 1. If these are absent, revise schedule before work begins. No company-wide development freeze is proposed.

name: Title 1
text: Task 2 - P1: Workflow and ownership

name: table-footnote
text: Suggested tools: a shared issue board and wiki. Retain existing tools if they satisfy the requirements.

Sources: [1], Task 2; [2], lecture slides 24, 28-36, 44. P1 addresses C1 and C3. WIP=3 is a starting experiment, not a universal limit; adjust using queue data. Definition of done includes peer review, required automated checks, documented migration impact, release/rollback instructions and a monitoring owner. Department heads retain staffing and specialist standards; the cross-functional pilot squad owns delivery. Escalation: a blocked item older than one working day goes to the transformation lead. Daily 10-minute squad check, weekly 30-minute review. Record decisions outside email.

title: Task 2 - P2: Build and test pipeline

name: Title 1
text: Task 2 - P2: Build and test pipeline

name: block-1-label
text: Weeks 3-5 | Dev lead + Test lead

name: block-1-text
text: Version application code, pipeline files and deployment scripts. Add peer review and required checks; integrate small changes daily. Proposed pilot tools: Git and GitHub Actions.

name: block-2-label
text: Executable path

name: block-2-text
text: Commit -> build -> unit tests -> integration tests against a test database -> acceptance checks -> versioned artifact -> staging. Failed checks block release and return to the change owner.

name: block-3-label
text: Acceptance and documents

name: block-3-text
text: The pilot critical journey passes automatically in staging. Test all three applications when shared schemas change. Publish pipeline setup, test ownership and a release checklist; retain exploratory acceptance testing.

Sources: [1], Task 2; [2], lecture slides 51-61. P2 addresses C2 and C3. GitHub Actions is a proposed tool choice, not a claim that the organization already uses it; retain an existing supported CI tool if adequate. Dev lead owns build and artifact traceability; Test lead owns risk-based regression selection and shared integration/acceptance checks. Use a dedicated test database with synthetic or sanitized data. Acceptance: a fresh checkout can build; deliberate test failures prevent artifact promotion; the same artifact is promoted from staging to production; reports are accessible to the squad. Target fast initial checks within 10 minutes, tune after observing the baseline. The knowledge produced by failing checks is converted into regression tests and troubleshooting notes.

name: Title 1
text: Task 2 - P3: Safe cloud releases

name: block-1-label
text: Weeks 4-6 | Ops lead + database owner

name: block-1-text
text: Create a reproducible staging environment and versioned infrastructure configuration; propose Terraform on existing Google Cloud. Add versioned migrations and compatibility checks for all three applications.

name: block-2-label
text: Production release control

name: block-2-text
text: Promote the tested artifact after a named Ops approver signs the checklist. Release one small change at a time; observe errors and latency. Revert the application if the agreed guardrail is breached.

name: block-3-label
text: Acceptance and recovery

name: block-3-text
text: Rehearse release, application rollback and database restore in staging. Publish a runbook with alert contacts. Keep incompatible schema removal out of the pilot; application rollback does not automatically undo data changes.

Sources: [1], Task 2; [2], lecture slides 54-61. P3 addresses C2 and C3. Appoint a database owner from Ops in week 1, with Dev/Test contributors. Terraform is a proposal, not a requirement or claim about current infrastructure. Concrete pilot guardrail proposal: stop promotion/rollback when application error rate exceeds 1% for 5 minutes, or p95 latency rises >20% above the measured pre-release baseline for 10 minutes. Ops and Sales must calibrate guardrails to traffic and service requirements before the first production release. Use recorded health checks when traffic is low. Do not claim those thresholds suit every app. Rollback objective: restore the last known-good app artifact within 10 minutes in a drill. Data recovery follows a separate backup/restore procedure; record backup completion, recovery point and restore duration. Acceptance requires all three applications passing schema compatibility tests and two successful staging deployment/rollback drills. The first live pilot release requires P2 and P3 acceptance plus a tested runbook.

name: Title 1
text: Task 2 - P4: Measurement and feedback

name: table-footnote
text: Sales reviews support themes weekly and puts user feedback into the shared backlog. Targets are proposals.

preview: Measure / definition | Collection and owner | Review / proposed target

text: Sources: [1], Tasks 2-3; [2], lecture slides 38-44 and 61. P4 is the Second Way and supports knowledge creation. Start collection in weeks 1-2, retain dashboards throughout rollout. Use Cloud Monitoring or existing supported monitoring, a versioned release log and shared review notes. CEO and squad review delivery/reliability together rather than reward feature count alone. Track test queue time and blocked-item age to check whether work merely moved between queues. Definitions are consistent within this presentation. Production recovery time and a planned rollback drill are different measurements. Report change failure rate as a fraction with sample counts, especially for low deployment frequency. These are design targets, not historical evidence. Baseline sources/coverage should be documented; do not invent missing timestamps.

name: Title 1
text: Task 2 - Resources and rollout gates

name: block-1-label
text: Proposed allocation | CEO + department heads

name: block-1-text
text: Pilot: two developers, one tester and one Ops engineer at 50% time; transformation lead at 20%. Sales product owner joins weekly prioritization. Confirm capacity and cloud budget in week 1.

name: block-2-label
text: Week 6 pilot gate | Ops + Test + Sales

name: block-2-text
text: Required checks pass; all-app schema tests pass; two staging release/rollback drills succeed; runbook and alert ownership are agreed. Then approve the first small production release.

name: block-3-label
text: Weeks 7-12 | Transformation lead

name: block-3-text
text: Collect two weeks of live pilot evidence, then onboard the second team in weeks 9-10 and the third in weeks 11-12 if gates pass. If reliability worsens, defer rollout and fix the constraint.

Source [1], Task 2; [2], lecture slides 28-36, 44, 61. Proposed allocation equals 2.2 FTE excluding the Sales owner, assuming the four pilot members each contribute 0.5 FTE plus the 0.2 FTE transformation lead. Role owners are company staff, not the three students. Week 1 CEO appoints accountable leads and agrees the budget cap for staging/tool use; Ops reports usage weekly. This reduces available feature capacity and should be reflected in the Sales backlog, rather than hiding the cost. Existing teams and departments remain in place during the pilot. Acceptance before onboarding: pilot ran for two weeks, metrics are recorded, no unresolved severe release-caused incident, checks and runbooks are understood by the receiving team. Rollout dates are conditional. Task 3 revises the sequence to add learning early, not after scale.

name: Title 1
text: Task 3 - Evaluate the original plan

name: table-footnote
text: Culture suitability is unknown. Interviews and observed behavior must test assumption A3.

preview: Existing item | Effect on experimentation / learning | Revision to the plan

text: Sources: [1], Task 3; [2], lecture slides 42-44. This is an explicit positive and negative evaluation of each original P1-P4 plan element. Consequences motivate operational changes, not just an added slogan. Do not infer that a separated organization has a proven punitive culture. CEO should test whether staff can raise mistakes safely, whether information is shared and whether reward systems conflict. Original week-6 release gates stay in place; delegate only reversible low-risk non-production experiments before production readiness.

name: Title 1
text: Task 3 - New learning actions

name: table-footnote
text: Resilience drills begin in staging only, with a named supervisor and an immediate stop/restore procedure.

preview: Action / owner / timing | Experiment or learning method | Evidence and acceptance

text: Sources: [1], Task 3; [2], lecture slides 42-44. L1-L3 add the Third Way. The 10% learning time is carved from the allocated pilot time in Task 2, not extra uncompensated work. The transformation lead protects it in the backlog. Example experiment: hypothesis that running integration tests per merge reduces test queue time; baseline first, trial for two weeks, compare queue age and defects, revert if checks become unreliable or queue age rises. Second experiment: WIP 3 versus WIP 2 using comparable work; adopt only if lead time improves without more incidents. Use a staging failure drill after P3 recovery rehearsal; no unsupervised production failure injection. Experiment records contain both supportive and contrary evidence. Near-miss reviews ensure learning continues when there are no live incidents.

name: Title 1
text: Task 3 - Knowledge and culture

name: block-1-label
text: How knowledge is created

name: block-1-text
text: Queue maps reveal constraints; test failures reveal defects; release drills expose recovery gaps; user feedback reveals needs; experiments compare a hypothesis with observed results.

name: block-2-label
text: How knowledge becomes organizational

name: block-2-text
text: An individual records the finding -> Dev/Test/Ops review it -> publish a test, runbook or decision -> another team reuses it -> verify reuse at the next monthly review.

name: block-3-label
text: Culture change | CEO + department heads

name: block-3-text
text: Model no-blame reviews, welcome early risk reports and protect learning time. Reward shared delivery and reliability outcomes. Survey trust monthly and act on concerns; do not rank individuals by deployment counts.

Sources: [1], Task 3 CEO questions; [2], lecture slides 42-44. The cultural diagnosis is conditional: if A3 is true, replace conflicting feature-only/uptime-only incentives; if not, reinforce existing shared incentives. CEO opens reviews by asking what the system made difficult, rather than who caused failure. Transformation lead uses a brief anonymous trust survey at baseline and monthly, e.g. whether people can raise mistakes safely; discuss aggregated themes. Dev/Test leads maintain a searchable learning index. Each new finding links to an owner, change and adoption evidence. Measure organizational learning through reuse and resolved action items, not document volume. Pairing creates individual knowledge; standardized tests and runbooks retain it after people move between teams.

name: Title 1
text: Task 3 - Revised integrated timeline

name: table-footnote
text: Revision: culture and protected learning now start before tooling and rollout. Scale remains conditional.

Sources: [1], Task 3 final iteration; [2], lecture slides 27-44 and 61. This final timeline supersedes the initial sequence where the Third Way had not been protected explicitly. Change in content: add L1-L3 and the culture/knowledge mechanism. Change in sequencing: trust and learning allocation in weeks 1-2, no-blame reviews/pairing in weeks 3-5, evidence-based scaling in weeks 9-12. Change in effort: reserve 10% of allocated pilot capacity for learning. Change in involved people: CEO models culture, Sales supplies feedback, specialist leads transfer learning across all teams. P1-P4 release and rollout gates remain binding. Delay scaling if severe incident actions remain open or the pilot is not stable; do not use the calendar alone as approval.

name: Title 1
text: Complete plan - Handover and review

name: block-1-label
text: Execution pack | Transformation lead

name: block-1-text
text: Deliver the value-stream map, squad charter, backlog/WIP policy, CI configuration, test ownership, database migration rules, release/restore runbooks, dashboard and experiment log. Each document has an owner.

name: block-2-label
text: Week 12 review | CEO + all department leads

name: block-2-text
text: Compare pilot outcomes with the recorded baseline; show sample sizes and unresolved risks. Check that another team can execute a release and reuse a documented lesson. Decide to scale, adjust or extend the pilot.

name: block-3-label
text: Main risks and responses

name: block-3-text
text: Feature capacity falls: Sales reprioritizes. Database coupling persists: retain compatibility checks. Trust is weak: leaders change incentives and review behavior. Results are inconclusive: collect more evidence before broader rollout.

Sources: [1], Tasks 2-3; [2], lecture slides 24, 28-44, 61. Operational handover means an identified person can follow the documented steps, not only understand the idea. Each pack item has a role owner: transformation lead owns charter/map/WIP; Dev lead CI; Test lead regression/schema test suite; database owner migrations and recovery; Ops lead release/restore/alerts; Sales owner prioritized backlog; Dev/Test leads learning index. Dry-run handover: the receiving team performs a staging release without the original author doing the steps, using the documentation; record gaps and repair them. Week 12 acceptance checks proposed targets, stability and learning reuse, with no claim that outcomes are guaranteed. For this exercise the brief permits assuming implemented practices function as described, but metrics are still presented as targets rather than fabricated observations.

name: block-3-text
